conversation.content: We're going to discuss designing a distributed message queue at massive scale. At this level, I'm interested in how you'd approach this as a strategic technical investment — build versus buy, organizational impact, multi-year evolution. Let's start: when would you build a custom message queue versus using something like Kafka or Pulsar?

Well, Kafka is the industry standard. I'd use Kafka for most use cases. You'd build custom if you need something Kafka doesn't support, like... uh, maybe very specific delivery guarantees or integration with proprietary systems.
Can you be more specific? LinkedIn, Uber, and Apple have all built custom messaging systems despite Kafka existing. What drove those decisions? What would the decision framework look like?

Right, so at massive scale the operational cost of managing open-source Kafka becomes significant. You need a dedicated team. If you're processing billions of messages, you might want tighter integration with your infrastructure — like your storage layer, monitoring, deployment system. And managed services like Confluent Cloud can get expensive at scale. So the build-versus-buy analysis is really about total cost of ownership over 3-5 years.
Let's say you've decided to build. How would you scope the first version? You can't build Kafka in one quarter.

I'd start with the core: publish and subscribe with partitioned topics. Support at-least-once delivery. Maybe skip features like transactions and compaction in V1. Focus on reliability and performance first.
How would you define 'reliability and performance' in concrete terms? What are the SLOs for this system?
The SLOs would be... high availability, like 99.99%. And low latency — maybe sub-10ms p99 for produce and consume. And zero message loss for acknowledged messages.

99.99% availability is 52 minutes of downtime per year. For a messaging backbone that everything depends on, is that sufficient? And sub-10ms p99 — is that realistic with disk persistence and replication?

Hmm, you're right — maybe 99.999% for the messaging backbone? Five nines. And on the latency, yeah, with disk writes and replication, maybe sub-10ms for the 95th percentile and sub-50ms for p99. It depends on the deployment — SSDs versus spinning disks, same-region replication versus cross-region.
Walk me through the high-level architecture of this system.

Standard architecture: broker nodes that store messages, a metadata layer for coordination — maybe using etcd or Raft consensus — producers that write to brokers, consumers that read from brokers. Topics are split into partitions, each partition is replicated across multiple brokers. One broker is the leader for each partition.
That describes Kafka's architecture. As a VP building this, what would you do differently? What lessons would you learn from Kafka's pain points?

Good question. Kafka's biggest pain point is ZooKeeper — it's a separate system to manage. I'd use an embedded Raft consensus layer in the brokers themselves, which is what Kafka is moving toward with KRaft. I'd also separate compute from storage — the brokers handle protocol and routing, but the actual log storage could be on a distributed file system or object storage like S3. That makes scaling storage independently of compute easier.
Interesting — tiered storage is a significant architectural choice. What are the trade-offs of putting log data on S3?

S3 gives you virtually unlimited storage and you don't manage disks. But the latency is much higher — maybe 50-200ms for a read. So you'd keep recent data on local SSDs for low-latency consumers and tier older data to S3 for replay and long-term retention. The trade-off is complexity — you need a caching layer and logic to transparently serve from either tier.
Now let's talk about the organizational side. How would you staff the team to build and operate this? What's the team structure?

I'd need a core team of maybe 8-10 engineers. A few focused on the broker/storage layer, a couple on the client libraries — producer and consumer SDKs — and a couple on operations, tooling, and monitoring. Plus a tech lead or architect overseeing the design.

8-10 engineers to build and operate a five-nines messaging backbone used by every team in the company? How do you handle oncall, production incidents, and customer support while also building new features?

Fair point — oncall alone eats capacity. I'd probably need 15-20 engineers total. Maybe split into a 'build' squad and a 'run' squad. The run squad handles oncall, incidents, and customer-facing support. The build squad works on new features. And they rotate periodically so knowledge stays shared.
How do you convince the VP of Product to give you 15-20 headcount for infrastructure that doesn't directly ship user-facing features?

It's an ROI argument. Every product team depends on messaging — if we use a managed service, the cost at our scale is significant. We could show the projected managed service bill versus the cost of the internal team. Plus, building in-house gives us competitive advantages — lower latency, tighter integration, features tailored to our needs.
What's your migration strategy? You presumably have existing systems on Kafka or RabbitMQ. How do you move the entire company to your new platform?

Migration is the hardest part. I'd make the new system wire-compatible with the Kafka protocol so existing clients work without code changes. Then migrate topic by topic, starting with low-risk topics. Run dual-write during migration — produce to both old and new systems — and shift consumers over gradually. Validate message counts match before decommissioning the old system.
We're running low on time. As you look 3 years out, how does this platform evolve? What's the strategic vision?

In 3 years... the platform becomes the unified data backbone. Beyond pub/sub, it supports stream processing — embedded stream queries on topic data, like a built-in Flink. We add serverless consumption — event-driven functions triggered by messages, reducing the boilerplate teams need. And multi-region replication for disaster recovery and global distribution. The vision is to be the one platform for all async communication in the company.

Thanks for the discussion. You showed decent technical intuition and some good strategic thinking, but I'd like to have seen more specificity in the ROI analysis and a more detailed team and migration plan.

strengths: Good insight on compute-storage separation and tiered storage trade-offs
Wire-compatible migration strategy showed practical thinking
weaknesses: Surface-level answers to most questions — described Kafka's architecture rather than demonstrating independent architectural thinking
No concrete ROI analysis or cost modeling — VP level should have numbers
Team structure discussion was thin — didn't address developer experience, platform adoption, or customer success
No capacity estimation or concrete performance modeling
Strategic vision was generic — 'unified platform' without specifics on competitive moat or business differentiation
